newsitem.title: USA: More Cuban Americans seen turning to Democrats.
newsitem.headline: More Cuban Americans seen turning to Democrats.

text.p: Cuban Americans, by repute staunch conservatives who scorn the Democrats as communist sympathisers, are showing themselves to be a community divided as the U.S. presidential election nears.
A range of views was highlighted this week by a dispute over aid to hurricane victims in Cuba and by President Bill Clinton's visit to south Florida, home to one million Cubans.

Early this month, Cuban-American Alex Penelas was elected as Dade County's executive mayor, a powerful new position. But Penelas, though supported by many Cuban-American Republicans during his campaign, is a Democrat.

No Democratic presidential candidate has carried Florida in 20 years and how a U.S. government deals with Cuban President Fidel Castro and his communist-ruled island is an emotive and politically volatile issue in Miami.
Passions ran high outside the hotel where Clinton spoke during a campaign swing through Florida this week.

Exile groups demonstrated for and against the U.S. trade embargo on Cuba and the Helms-Burton Law introduced in March to enable U.S. citizens to take legal action against companies investing in property confiscated after the 1959 revolution. Insults and oaths flew across the police barricades.
Marcos Correa, secretary general of the Alliance of Cuban Workers, said many Cuban-Americans were Democrats but that the right wing had control of the community and media.
"They are rich people. They talk about war. When the United States lifts the blockade, Castro won't have excuses anymore," he said.
On the other side, demonstrators, some dressed in the combat fatigues of paramilitary groups, called the Democrat supporters "traitors" and "cockroaches."

Neil Nunez, 58, who said he arrived in Miami in 1980 after spending 10 years in a Cuban jail, said he was angry at the president for shifting U.S. immigration policy to send back to Cuba boat people picked up at sea.
"Clinton is always making zig-zags. He sent back our brothers who came from Cuba. We will all vote Dole," he said.
That night Clinton made a surprise visit to Little Havana where he was cheered by supporters, booed by some folk and met leaders from both sides.
Conservative Cubans have reviled Democrats since President John Kennedy failed to send in air cover for the doomed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.

But Tuesday night's scene in Little Havana was a change from the days when Ronald Reagan was idolised by the community -- which renamed a street after him -- during the Central American wars in the 1980s.
Dole does not appear to have captured their imagination in quite the same way.

Jorge Mas Canosa, the leading figure in the conservative camp, was quoted on Spanish-language WCMQ radio as saying he would give Clinton "no better than average grade" on Cuba but Dole "hasn't done any better a job."
Recent polls estimated Clinton could win 40 percent of the Cuban-American vote, up from 22 percent in 1992.

During Clinton's visit, a debate raged over sending aid to Cubans hit by Hurricane Lili. Those anxious to help relatives and countrymen collected relief supplies. Others opposed the drive, saying aid to Cuba was aid to Castro.
